mcqs.q: Finishing and polishing is considered the:
opts: Last (but very important) step of the restorative process
mcqs.explain: Finishing and polishing is the last step of the restorative process, yet one of the most important for a natural look.

mcqs.q: Improper finishing/polishing of a restoration can lead to:
opts: Plaque accumulation, gingival irritation, staining and recurrent caries
mcqs.explain: A poorly finished surface accumulates plaque, irritates the gingiva, stains, and can lead to recurrent caries and periodontal problems.

mcqs.q: FINISHING is best defined as:
opts: Transforming a restoration from a rough to a refined form (contour/smoothness)
mcqs.explain: Finishing transforms the restoration from rough to refined — removing marginal irregularities, defining contours and smoothing roughness.

mcqs.q: POLISHING is best defined as:
opts: Producing a shiny, mirror-like surface that reflects light like enamel
mcqs.explain: Polishing produces a shiny, mirror-like surface that reflects light similarly to natural enamel.

mcqs.q: A smooth, well-polished restoration benefits ORAL HEALTH because it:
opts: Accumulates less debris/bacteria and is easier to keep clean
mcqs.explain: A smoother restoration accumulates less food debris and pathogenic bacteria, making oral hygiene easier.

mcqs.q: A well-polished restoration improves ORAL FUNCTION because:
opts: Food glides more freely over occlusal/embrasure surfaces
mcqs.explain: With a smooth surface, food glides freely over the occlusal and embrasure surfaces during mastication.

mcqs.q: How do finishing burs differ from cutting burs?
opts: Finer blades, smaller size, and MORE blades
Coarser blades and fewer of them
mcqs.explain: Finishing-bur blades are finer, their sizes smaller, and their number of blades greater than cutting burs.

mcqs.q: A CUTTING bur usually has how many blades?
mcqs.explain: Cutting burs usually have 6–10 blades; finishing burs have 12–40.

mcqs.q: A FINISHING bur usually has how many blades?
mcqs.explain: Finishing burs have 12–40 blades (the number of blades on a bur is usually even).

mcqs.q: Which coated diamond burs are typically used for FINISHING?
mcqs.explain: Yellow- and white-coded (fine/superfine) diamond burs are used for finishing.

mcqs.q: Abrasive finishing/polishing discs should be used:
opts: Sequentially from coarse → medium → fine → superfine
mcqs.explain: Discs (e.g. Sof-Lex, coated with Al₂O₃/SiC) are used sequentially from coarse to medium to fine to superfine to generate a smooth surface.

mcqs.q: Abrasive polishing discs are generally:
mcqs.explain: The thin abrasive layer remains effective only briefly, so the discs are single-use/disposable.

mcqs.q: Finishing/polishing of an AMALGAM restoration should be:
mcqs.explain: Amalgam finishing is delayed ~24 hours after condensation, because crystallisation and full compressive strength are not yet attained.

mcqs.q: Why is amalgam not finished immediately?
opts: Crystallisation is incomplete and compressive strength is not yet attained
It is already at full strength
mcqs.explain: Before full set, crystallisation is incomplete and compressive strength is low, so early finishing could damage the restoration.

mcqs.q: In the rubber amalgam-polishing system, 'Brownies' are:
mcqs.explain: In the rubber system, Brownies are coarse and Greenies are fine.

mcqs.q: 'Greenies' in the rubber polishing system are:
mcqs.explain: Greenies are the fine rubber polishers, used after the coarse Brownies.

mcqs.q: A low-cost final amalgam polish can use:
opts: Pumice (with water) then tin oxide on a prophylaxis cup
mcqs.explain: Pumice mixed with water, followed by tin oxide on a prophy cup in a low-speed handpiece, is a low-cost polishing option (though it splatters).

mcqs.q: Gingival/proximal overhangs are best removed/smoothed with:
mcqs.explain: Narrow finishing strips are used to remove overhangs and smooth the gingival/proximal surface.

mcqs.q: For gross contouring of a concave occlusal surface, you can use a:
mcqs.explain: Gross contouring/finishing of the concave occlusal surface uses a round or oval 12-bladed carbide or a finishing diamond.

mcqs.q: The finishing bur shown being used on the tooth is intended to:
opts: Refine the contour/margins and smooth the restoration
mcqs.explain: Finishing burs refine the contour and margins and smooth the restoration surface, not cut new tooth structure.

mcqs.q: Why is the number of blades on a bur usually EVEN?
opts: Balanced (opposing) blades give smoother, more concentric cutting
mcqs.explain: Burs are made with an even number of blades so opposing blades balance the bur for smoother, concentric cutting/finishing.

saqs.a: Finishing = rough → refined (remove irregularities, define contour, smooth). Polishing = a shiny, mirror-like, enamel-like surface.
Plaque accumulation, gingival irritation, staining, poor esthetics → recurrent caries and periodontal problems.

saqs.q: List the objectives of finishing and polishing.
How do finishing burs differ from cutting burs (incl. blade numbers)?
saqs.a: Finishing burs have finer, smaller, more blades (12–40) vs cutting burs (6–10).

saqs.q: How are abrasive discs used, and are they reusable?
saqs.a: Used sequentially coarse → medium → fine → superfine; they are single-use/disposable.

saqs.q: When is amalgam finished/polished and why the delay?
saqs.a: After ~24 hours (fully set); before that crystallisation/compressive strength is incomplete.

saqs.q: Name the rubber amalgam-polishing components and a low-cost final polish.
saqs.a: Brownies (coarse), Greenies (fine); low-cost = pumice then tin oxide on a prophy cup.
